CREATORS.summary: Ads were still made by agencies, but the agency business changed owner and changed shape. Between 1977 and 1992 the number of US advertising-agency establishments with payroll rose from 8,089 to 13,879 and industry billings rose from $15.5B to $69.6B (Economic Census). At the same time ownership concentrated into four listed holding companies: Interpublic (already public), Omnicom (formed in 1986 from BBDO, Doyle Dane Bernbach and Needham Harper), Saatchi & Saatchi (which bought Ted Bates for $450M in 1986), and WPP (J. Walter Thompson 1987, The Ogilvy Group 1989). Consolidation at the top, proliferation at the bottom: small creative shops, media-buying specialists and direct-marketing agencies multiplied under the holding companies. A second creator class scaled beside the agencies: the direct-mail production industry, which the Census counted separately as SIC 7331 with 3,900 establishments, 81,000 employees and $8.3B of receipts by 1993. Media commissions still paid for most of it, but their share of agency income fell from 61.3% in 1987 to 54.2% in 1992 as fees and unbundled services grew.

BUYERS.summary: Four pools of money bought advertising in this era, and they behaved differently. National brand advertisers (packaged goods, autos, tobacco, beer, fast food) bought reach through agencies on commission and supplied 58.1% of measured spend by 1993. Local retail money - car dealers, supermarkets, department stores, restaurants - supplied 41.9% and dominated the media it bought: 88.7% of newspaper revenue and 87% of Yellow Pages revenue was local in 1993. Classified money came from individuals and small businesses buying by the line with no agency in between. Direct-response money came from catalogers, publishers, insurers, credit-card issuers, record and book clubs, fundraisers and, from the mid-1980s, infomercial marketers; it was bought against a measured cost per order rather than a cost per thousand. The era's marginal new buyer class was the database-driven direct marketer - the advertiser who bought a rented list plus a ZIP-code cluster instead of a national audience. One large caveat: the measured-media total excludes trade and consumer promotion, and by 1992 trade promotion alone took 44.9% of packaged-goods marketing-communications budgets, so the biggest single shift in national brand money during the 1980s happened outside the advertising numbers entirely.

claims.statement: Direct mail took 33.3% of all US national advertising spend in 1993 ($27,266M of $81,867M) - more than all national television combined (network $10,209M + national spot $7,800M + syndication $1,576M + cable networks $3,295M = $22,880M). Caveat: Coen books direct mail as entirely national and its figure includes postage and production, not just a media rate.
claims.unit: percent of US national ad spend

SELLERS.summary: The three broadcast networks stopped being the market. Their combined prime-time share fell from over 90% in the mid-1970s to 61% by the 1988-89 season while cable's share reached 20%, and the number of national cable networks went from 28 in 1980 to 79 in 1990. But the cable networks were weak sellers of advertising: the US cable industry took $26.9B of revenue in 1993 and only $2.6B of it - 9.8% - was advertising, because cable's real customer was the subscriber. Newspapers remained the single largest medium at $32.0B, sold locally by chains with monopoly positions in most metros. Two sellers most histories skip were enormous here. The Regional Bell Operating Companies, handed the directory business at the 1984 AT&T divestiture, sold $9.5B of Yellow Pages advertising in 1993 - more than radio and more than magazines - through door-to-door sales forces on annual contracts. And the US Postal Service, which collected $9.8B of third-class postage revenue in FY1993 against $2.4B in FY1980, was effectively the distribution monopoly underneath the country's third-largest medium. Alongside them sat a new layer of data sellers - Claritas, Donnelley Marketing, R.L. Polk, list brokers and compilers - who sold not audience but addresses.

MEDIUM.summary: The share chart of this era does not look like the story usually told about it. Newspapers fell from 28.9% of US measured spend in 1976 to 22.7% in 1993 but stayed the single largest medium until 1992, when total television (broadcast plus cable) first passed them, $31.1B to $30.7B; broadcast television alone was still behind newspapers in 1993. Cable, the era's headline, went from $72M in 1980 to $4.45B in 1993 - 62x growth, but still only 3.2% of the market. The medium that actually grew into the gap was direct mail: from $4.79B (14.4%) in 1976 to $27.27B (19.3%) in 1993, the third-largest medium in the country and the single largest national medium. Yellow Pages, broken out by Coen only from 1980, reached $9.5B and passed both radio and magazines. Radio drifted from 7.0% to 6.7% and was never close to the top. Behind the direct-mail line sat a physical fact: US third-class mail volume more than doubled from 30.4 billion pieces in FY1980 to 65.8 billion in FY1993, from 28.6% to 38.4% of everything the Postal Service delivered.

SCALE.summary: Measured US advertising spend grew from $33.3B in 1976 to $141.0B in 1993 - 4.2x nominal, an 8.9% compound annual rate, faster than nominal GDP. As a share of GDP it climbed from about 1.8% in 1976 to a plateau of 2.3% in 1986-89, then eased to about 2.1% by 1993; the same series would peak at 2.3-2.4% in 2000, so the era's ad intensity is a rise, not the top. National money was 58.1% of the 1993 total and local money 41.9%. Two boundaries matter for anyone reading these numbers. First, they are measured media only: trade and consumer promotion, which by 1992 took nearly half of packaged-goods marketing budgets, are not in them. Second, the Coen series prices inventory at rate-card list prices rather than transaction prices, and it books direct mail (postage, lists and production included) as an entirely national medium - which is why the later Magna backcast puts direct mail near 12% of 1980 spend where Coen puts it at 14.2%. The era also contains one clean macro event: 1991 was the first nominal decline in US advertising spend since 1961.

PRICING.summary: Two pricing regimes ran side by side and neither one was an auction. Brand media was priced per thousand against a rate card, negotiated in an annual upfront for network television and in scatter for what was left, with the agency taking a commission on the gross. The received story is that the 15% commission died in the 1980s; the Economic Census says otherwise. Commissions actually received on media billings were 14.13% in 1977, 13.92% in 1982, 14.16% in 1987 and 13.18% in 1992 - and only then collapsed, to 10.98% by 1997. What eroded first was the mix, not the rate: the ANA's tracking studies show 71% of large national advertisers on commissions in 1982 and 61% by 1994, with labour fees rising from 8% to 31%. The pressure came from price: the Universal McCann composite media unit cost index rose from 58.0 in 1977 to 149.9 in 1992 while the GDP deflator roughly doubled, so a fixed percentage of media cost was buying advertisers a shrinking amount of work. The other regime priced response. Direct mail was bought per thousand pieces - list rental at $25-30 per thousand for compiled names and $50-80 for response names in the early 1990s, production from about 40 cents a piece, postage rising from 7.9 cents to 14.9 cents per third-class piece across the era - and judged on cost per order at a 2-3% response. Yellow Pages was sold on annual contracts by size and position. Classified was sold by the line, self-serve, with no commission to anyone.

claims.statement: Media commissions actually received by US advertising agencies as a percentage of media billings were 14.13% in 1977, 13.92% in 1982, 14.16% in 1987 and 13.18% in 1992, before falling to 10.98% in 1997. The 15% commission survived this era largely intact; its collapse comes after it.

MEASUREMENT.summary: Every price in this market rested on somebody's count, and in 1987 the count changed. Nielsen replaced diaries and household set meters with people meters as the national currency for the 1987-88 season, and measured prime-time viewing fell roughly 10% overnight; CBS and ABC each lost 13%, NBC 4%, and the Saturday-morning children's audience fell by 20% to 50% against about $150M of network children's advertising. The networks owed make-goods in scatter time worth more than the upfront time they had sold, and they attacked the panel's composition - 33% of people-meter homes had pay cable against 26% of the population. Nothing about the audience had changed; only the instrument had. On the direct-response side the counting was of a different kind: keyed coupons, source codes and toll-free numbers gave an exact cost per order, and from 1979 IRI's BehaviorScan wired two towns - scanners in 15 supermarkets, 2,000 recruited households each, with cable ad cut-ins to the same homes - to produce the first electronic single-source link between an ad exposure and a purchase. The market's own aggregate measure had a bias too: the McCann series that everyone quoted was built on rate-card list prices rather than transaction prices, and treated direct mail as wholly national, which is why the later Magna backcast disagrees with it on direct mail's share by two to six points.

claims.statement: Nielsen's people meters, which became the national television currency in September 1987, measured about 10% fewer people watching network prime time than the previous method: CBS and ABC each down 13%, NBC down 4%.

TARGETING.summary: Targeting in this era moved from demographics to geography-as-demographics, and the unit of precision became the neighbourhood rather than the person. Jonathan Robbin's Claritas took the 1970 census, reallocated it from census geography onto all roughly 36,000 five-digit ZIP codes, and clustered them into 40 named types - PRIZM, the Potential Rating Index for Zip Markets. Rivals followed with ClusterPlus (Donnelley) and ACORN (CACI), and SRI's VALS added a psychographic axis from 1978. The 1983 arrival of ZIP+4 cut the addressable unit below the ZIP again. Combined with rented and compiled lists, merge/purge de-duplication, and the customer databases that airlines and card issuers were building from their own transaction systems, this let a mailer choose which streets to buy. The ceiling was hard: a 2% response on a rented list means 98% waste, and the industry's own worked examples show a million-piece mailing at 60 cents a piece needing 2% response at a $100 order value just to clear a profit. Cable supplied the other half of the story - 79 national networks by 1990 against three broadcast networks in 1976, each sold as a psychographic slice (music, sports, news, children, women). Nobody in this era could target intent. They could target the mailbox on a particular block, and the channel a particular kind of household watched.

claims.statement: PRIZM classified all roughly 36,000 US five-digit ZIP codes into 40 lifestyle clusters, built by reallocating 1970 census tabulations from census geography onto ZIP geography - the era's dominant geodemographic targeting system.

sources.name: Griffith, 'When the New Magic was New: The Claritas Corporation and the Clustering of America', IEEE Annals of the History of Computing
Overview of Geodemography (Robbin's ZIP reallocation and 40-category classification)

claims.statement: PRIZM's commercial launch year is contested: secondary sources give 1974, 1976 and 1978, with Claritas itself founded in 1971 or 1974. The record uses 1978 as the central launch year with the interval running back to 1974 rather than picking a winner.

sources.name: Grokipedia, 'Claritas Prizm' (launch 1978, 40 clusters)
Griffith, IEEE Annals of the History of Computing, 'When the New Magic was New' (system built 1974)

claims.statement: US households received about 253 pieces of third-class advertising mail per person per year by 1993, against 133 in 1980 - roughly 660 pieces a year for an average household, the physical footprint of geodemographic targeting.
claims.unit: third-class pieces per person per year

sources.name: US Postal Service, via Statistical Abstract of the United States 1995, table 925 (per capita third-class mail)

claims.statement: The best-targeted medium of the era still missed 98 out of 100 recipients: a 2% response rate on a rented list was the working definition of a successful direct-mail campaign, with 2-3% treated as good.

sources.name: Encyclopedia of American Industries, 'SIC 7331 Direct Mail Advertising Services'
DMA, Statistical Fact Book 2001 (cost-of-acquisition worked examples use 1-2% response on 1,000,000-piece drops)

claims.statement: Television targeting precision rose from 3 national channels in 1976 to 79 national cable networks by 1990, each addressing a self-selected niche - the supply side of segmentation.

sources.name: Brad Adgate, 'The Rise And Fall Of Cable Television', Forbes (citing NCTA)

events.title: WTCG becomes the first national superstation
events.desc: Ted Turner's Atlanta independent WTCG went up on RCA's Satcom 1 at 1pm Eastern, relayed to four cable systems in Nebraska, Virginia, Alabama and Kansas. HBO had used satellite first, in September 1975, but as a pay service; WTCG was the first advertising-supported station distributed nationally by satellite, and within two years reached cable systems in all fifty states. It created the thing cable advertising needed: a national audience that was not a broadcast network.

events.title: ESPN launches
events.desc: The first national cable network built around a single demographic slice rather than a general audience. ESPN, CNN (June 1980), MTV (August 1981) and Nickelodeon turned cable from a retransmission utility into a set of separately priced niche audiences. Cable advertising was $72M in 1980 and $4,451M by 1993.

events.title: MTV launches
events.desc: The clearest demonstration that a cable channel could be sold as a psychographic rather than a geography or a daypart. Advertisers bought MTV to reach a defined kind of person nationally - the segmentation logic that PRIZM was applying to the mailbox, applied to the dial.

events.title: ZIP+4 cuts the addressable unit below the ZIP code
events.desc: The Postal Service introduced the nine-digit ZIP+4, subdividing the roughly 36,000 five-digit ZIPs that PRIZM had clustered into far smaller delivery segments. Combined with cheaper computing, merge/purge de-duplication and commercial list compilation, it moved direct-mail targeting from the town to the block face.

events.title: AT&T divestiture hands Yellow Pages to the Regional Bells
events.desc: The Bell System broke up and the directory business went to the seven Regional Bell Operating Companies, turning a monopoly by-product into a competitive industry with door-to-door sales forces and annual contracts. Yellow Pages advertising went from $2.9B in 1980 to $9.5B in 1993, larger than radio and larger than magazines - the closest structural ancestor of paid search: businesses paying for placement against category-level intent.

claim.statement: US Yellow Pages advertising revenue grew from $2,900M in 1980 to $9,517M in 1993, a 3.3x rise across the era.

sources.name: Coen Structured Advertising Expenditure Dataset, workbook

events.title: FCC lifts commercial time limits and the program-length commercial ban
events.desc: The Commission deregulated commercial television, removing maximum advertising minutes per hour and the long-standing bar on program-length commercials. Stations and cable networks could now sell whole half-hours, which created the infomercial and gave direct-response advertisers a measurable television format bought on remnant and per-inquiry terms. The children's-programming half of the decision was remanded by the D.C. Circuit in 1987 and reversed by Congress in the Children's Television Act of 1990.

events.title: The Big Bang: agency holding companies take over
events.desc: Omnicom was formed from BBDO, Doyle Dane Bernbach and Needham Harper, and Saatchi & Saatchi bought Ted Bates Worldwide for about $450M. WPP followed with J. Walter Thompson in 1987 and The Ogilvy Group in 1989. Ownership of the agency business concentrated into four listed holding companies while the number of US agency establishments went on rising - from 8,089 in 1977 to 13,879 in 1992.

claim.statement: Saatchi & Saatchi acquired Ted Bates Worldwide for about $450M in 1986, the largest agency acquisition to that date.

sources.name: Encyclopedia.com, 'Saatchi & Saatchi'

events.title: Fox Broadcasting launches
events.desc: The first viable fourth national broadcast network since DuMont, built out of independent stations and aimed at a younger, narrower audience than ABC, CBS or NBC. Fox's arrival, together with syndication (which Coen first breaks out in 1980 and which reached $1,576M by 1993), meant national television money no longer had only three doors.

events.title: Nielsen people meters become the television currency
events.desc: For the 1987-88 season Nielsen replaced diaries and household set meters with people meters as the national currency. Measured network prime-time viewing fell about 10% at once - CBS and ABC each 13%, NBC 4% - and the Saturday-morning children's audience by 20% to 50%, against roughly $150M of children's advertising. Networks paid make-goods in scatter inventory worth more than the upfront time they had sold, and disputed the panel's cable skew. The clearest pre-digital proof that the counting method sets the price.

claim.statement: The 1987 people-meter switchover cut measured network prime-time audience by about 10% overnight, with CBS and ABC each down 13%.
claim.unit: percent drop in measured prime-time audience

sources.name: Christian Science Monitor, 'For TV networks, People Meter is a profit eater', 6 January 1988

events.title: US advertising spend falls for the first time since 1961
events.desc: Measured US advertising spend fell 1.24% in nominal terms, from $129,968M to $128,352M - the first nominal decline in the Coen series in thirty years. Newspapers took the worst of it, falling from $32,281M to $30,409M; direct mail, Yellow Pages and cable all kept growing straight through the recession, which is the era's structural story in one year of data.

claim.statement: Measured US advertising spend fell 1.24% in 1991, the first nominal decline since 1961.

sources.name: Coen Structured Advertising Expenditure Dataset, workbook

boundary_notes: Shared with era 3 (1950-1975): the era opens with measured US ad spend at $33.3B in 1976 (Coen), about 1.8% of GDP; newspapers are the #1 medium at 28.9% and television is second at 20.2%; the 15% commission is intact (Economic Census puts commissions actually received at 14.13% of media billings in 1977); Nielsen household meters and diaries are the television currency; the upfront/scatter structure and the 30-second spot are inherited, not invented, here. The mail-order and keyed-coupon accountability tradition (Ward, Sears, Hopkins) belongs to eras 1-2; era 4 owns only its database upgrade. Yellow Pages is inside Coen's 'Miscellaneous' before 1980, so no pre-1980 directory figure should be attributed to this record. Shared with era 5 (1994-2001): the era closes with measured US ad spend at $141.0B in 1993, about 2.1% of GDP; direct mail at $27.27B is the third-largest medium and the largest single national medium; Yellow Pages is at $9.52B and near its share peak (Magna puts directories' peak share at almost 9% in 1991); newspaper classified is estimated at about $11.2B and still climbing toward its documented $19.6B peak in 2000; cable advertising is $4.45B, 3.2% of the market; the Big Three's prime-time share is around 60%; agency media commissions are 13.18% of billings in 1992 and collapse to 10.98% by 1997, so the commission's death belongs to era 5, not here; internet advertising is not yet a line in any series (Coen opens the internet category in 1990 but with no meaningful spend before 1996). Series warning for R2: Coen is the only per-medium series covering the whole of 1976-1993; Magna's backcast starts in 1980, is built top-down from supplier revenue rather than bottom-up from rate-card billings, and disagrees with Coen on direct mail by two to six points of share. The 1990 total itself differs by 0.29% between Coen vintages ($129,590M in 2001, $129,968M in 2009).
